articles.title: API documentation examples and how to rewrite unclear endpoint docs
articles.excerpt: Most API docs are written by the people who built the API. That's why they're accurate and still hard to use. The author already knows what a "resource" is, which field is required and why the call re…
articles.body: Most API docs are written by the people who built the API. That's why they're accurate and still hard to use. The author already knows what a "resource" is, which field is required and why the call returns 409. The reader doesn't. This post walks through API documentation examples for the parts first time users read most. Endpoint summaries, parameter tables, request and response samples, error docs and auth steps. Each section shows a terse version and a clearer rewrite. What a reader needs from an endpoint page A developer landing on an endpoint page wants to answer five questions fast. What does this call do? What do I have to send? What will I get back? What can go wrong? Can I copy something that works? If your page answers those in that order, you're ahead of most docs.
articles.author: Gabe Garcia

articles.title: Resilience Is the New UX: Building Offline-First Real-Time Apps That Survive Network Failure
articles.excerpt: Originally published on tamiz.pro. The era of assuming a stable network is over. Users move through tunnels, elevators, and spotty mobile coverage, yet they expect real-time collaboration to feel inst…
articles.body: Originally published on tamiz.pro . The era of assuming a stable network is over. Users move through tunnels, elevators, and spotty mobile coverage, yet they expect real-time collaboration to feel instant. The gap between optimistic UI updates and server truth is where UX dies. Offline-first is not a feature; it's an architectural stance that treats network failure as a normal state, not an exception. This deep-dive explores the core principles, data structures, and sync strategies you need to build real-time apps that don't fall apart when the network does. Table of Contents 1. The Offline-First Mindset 2. Core Principles: Local-First, Sync-Later 3. Data Layer: Local Storage and IndexedDB 4. Sync Engines: The Heart of Offline-First 5. Conflict Resolution with CRDTs 6.
articles.author: Tamiz Uddin

articles.excerpt: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine. Old notes are little ghosts: they still contain memories, but their links can point to names that no l…
articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine . What I Built Old notes are little ghosts: they still contain memories, but their links can point to names that no longer exist. VaultRelink helps a person find those lost connections in a local Markdown archive. It scans [[wiki links]] , finds missing targets, ranks existing notes, and shows real excerpts and suggested replacements in a local HTML report. It never edits the vault; a human decides what to do. Demo Watch the illustrated walkthrough . The video illustrates the actual fictional-vault run; it is not a screen recording. The included fictional demo has a broken link to a garden of memories.

articles.body: ProvenPin is a library of tested code recipes for AI coding models. Each recipe pins exact package versions, runs its own tests in a clean environment, and carries a receipt showing when it last passed. The goal is to help free and cheap models write code that actually runs. It is served over a free MCP server, no API key, no signup. This was a quality week rather than a growth week. The live health endpoint shows 556 recipes, up from 555 last Thursday. Most of the work went into making the checks and answers more trustworthy. Here is what shipped (Oct 23 to 29). Strict type-checks for TypeScript recipes A recipe can run and pass its tests and still have type errors your editor will flag. CI now runs a strict tsc type-check on every TypeScript recipe a pull request adds or changes.

articles.title: Amazon Prototype Uses Robot Manipulation to Cut Item Damage
articles.excerpt: Originally published on The Daily Flare. Robot manipulation is moving beyond simple pickup: an Amazon prototype uses three-dimensional scene understanding and pinch grasps to handle selected items wit…
articles.body: Originally published on The Daily Flare . Robot manipulation is moving beyond simple pickup: an Amazon prototype uses three-dimensional scene understanding and pinch grasps to handle selected items with less damage in preliminary tests. Reading a cluttered scene Picking up an object is only one part of handling it. A robot also has to find the intended item, work out how it sits among other objects, choose a place to make contact and keep control while moving it. Those steps become difficult when shelves or bins are crowded, or when other objects block part of the target. Amazon Science describes research aimed at helping robots understand cluttered environments in three dimensions, identify specific items and retrieve them safely.

articles.title: NocoDB shared views need a permission review before they spread
articles.excerpt: NocoDB shared views need a permission review before they spread NocoDB makes it easy to expose a base, table or view as a shared application without giving every viewer a full account. That is often t…
articles.body: NocoDB shared views need a permission review before they spread NocoDB makes it easy to expose a base, table or view as a shared application without giving every viewer a full account. That is often the point. It also creates a gap between "the NocoDB login is protected" and "a shared URL can read these records." Security reviews should inspect both the base permission model and the public sharing path. NocoDB's documentation describes shared views and forms as public-access features. It also describes role-based access at workspace, base and table levels, with record-level security available in some editions. API tokens have permission scopes and expiration, and the effective permission is the intersection of the user's role and the token's permissions.

articles.title: Cosmic graveyard of zombie planets offers a grisly warning about our own solar system's fate
articles.excerpt: Two zombie exoplanets that rose from the grave to shuffle through the gory remains of their fellow planets may just agree with these immortal words from horror maestro Stephen King.
articles.body: "Sometimes dead is better." Who can forget the immortal words of Jud Crandall, delivered by the incomparable Fred Gwynne in the 1989 film adaptation of Stephen King's Pet Sematary? Turns out Crandall could have been talking about somewhere just as otherworldly as the cursed Chumash burial ground at the heart of one of King's most terrifying works of fiction. That's because astronomers have discovered two husks of two zombie planets shuffling through the gory remains of what was once their planetary neighbors around a long-deceased star, or white dwarf. The shattered planets were revealed by a clear gap in the debris around the white dwarf J1328−1450, located around 1,600 light-years away from Earth.

articles.excerpt: When companies began approaching NASA’s Langley Research Center, asking to be included in the In-Space Servicing, Assembly, and Manufacturing (ISAM) State of Play for access to competitive intelligenc…
articles.body: 3 min read Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater) When companies began approaching NASA’s Langley Research Center, asking to be included in the In-Space Servicing, Assembly, and Manufacturing (ISAM) State of Play for access to competitive intelligence, the team knew they had crossed an inflection point. “We’ve had some unnamed companies ask if we have any proprietary information,” says Dale Arney, senior team lead for the ISAM Technology Portfolio at NASA Langley. The answer is “no,” but that impartiality is precisely what makes the State of Play invaluable to an industry trying to understand a rapidly expanding field. articles.excerpt: Today on Decoder, I’m joined by Joey Brookhart, an analyst at the chip and AI research firm SemiAnalysis, to help me dig into the story inside the numbers of the Anthropic IPO filing — a document know…
articles.body: Today on Decoder , I’m joined by Joey Brookhart, an analyst at the chip and AI research firm SemiAnalysis, to help me dig into the story inside the numbers of the Anthropic IPO filing — a document known as an S-1. Anthropic just filed its S-1 to go public on the Nasdaq, and it could start trading as soon as next month at a valuation of anywhere between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion. That would immediately make it one of the most valuable companies on the planet. But the price tag really isn’t the whole story here. The S-1 document published earlier this week is hundreds upon hundreds of pages filled with details that finally paint a picture of the economics of a frontier AI lab.

articles.title: We urgently need to monitor AI agents’ actions in real time
articles.excerpt: This summer, hundreds of OpenAI agents tried to cheat on a cybersecurity test. They broke out of their test environment and successfully hacked Hugging Face, a site that they believed held clues about…
articles.body: This summer, hundreds of OpenAI agents tried to cheat on a cybersecurity test. They broke out of their test environment and successfully hacked Hugging Face, a site that they believed held clues about how they’d be graded. Around the same time, another OpenAI agent accessed private files from an Australian government website. It’s a problem that’s by no means confined to OpenAI. In the months since, Anthropic, Google, and Meta have also disclosed incidents in which their agents have gone off track. And worryingly, in many cases the agents eluded the very researchers and safety teams tasked with monitoring them.  AI agents are taking unauthorized actions, and the companies building and running them are mostly relying on luck and hindsight to mitigate any harmful impacts.
